Ladies and gentlemen, fellow defenders of liberty,

We stand at a crossroads where the architecture of our public square has been rebuilt not by the people, not by our legislatures or courts, but by a handful of private companies whose decisions now shape what millions of us can see, say, and learn. The keys to conversation, to culture, to political debate, rest in the hands of corporate moderators and opaque algorithms. This concentration of communicative power presents a grave danger to the foundations of free expression and to the democratic experiment itself.

Freedom of speech is not an abstract ornament to be displayed when convenient. It is the lifeblood of a free society — messy, imperfect, sometimes painful, but essential. It protects not only the speech we love and the causes we cheer, but the speech we loathe. If we permit private actors to set the boundaries of acceptable discourse without law, without transparency, without accountability, we trade a free people for a curated, corporate-approved version of reality.

Yes, there are voices we find repugnant. There are groups and ideas that pursue hatred, division, and falsehood. We must confront them, condemn them, and counter them with truth and decency. But to shut them out of public platforms by private fiat is to let private power decide who may participate in civic life. That power can — and at times will — be used to silence dissenting minorities, political outsiders, whistleblowers, and unorthodox thinkers. Today it may muzzle a hateful organization; tomorrow it may silence a reformer, a journalist, or a dissenter whose opinions those in power dislike.

The principle that must guide us is simple and profound: the law, not private preference, should define the limits of permissible speech in our digital public square. If speech is legal under democratically enacted statutes, platforms should not unilaterally erase it from public view. Instead, a transparent, rule-based system — rooted in due process, judicial oversight, and clear standards — should govern content moderation. Platforms that serve as the modern conduits of public discourse should be compelled by law to host lawful expression, while being subject to reasonable obligations: transparency about their processes, mechanisms for appeal, and safeguards against abuse.

Let us be crystal clear: insisting that legally permissible speech be hosted is not an endorsement of hateful content. It is a defense of the process that keeps our liberties alive. We can and must condemn harmful ideas and work tirelessly to diminish their influence through counter-speech, education, and civic engagement. The answer to hatred is not silence; it is exposure, exposure that allows truth to defeat falsehood in the marketplace of ideas.

Moreover, legal clarity protects platforms themselves and the public alike. A statutory framework that treats major online services as neutral carriers for lawful content — subject to anti-discrimination rules and due-process requirements — creates predictable rules of the road. Platforms would know their obligations and rights; users would know their protections; the courts would retain the role of upholding fundamental liberties. This is not an abdication of responsibility. It is the reassertion of democratic governance over private censorship.

We must demand transparency. We must insist on robust appeals processes when accounts are suspended or content removed. We must require regular reporting on takedowns, the criteria used, and the demographics affected. We must protect the vulnerable, who are often the last to be heard when decisions are made behind closed doors by platform staff and opaque algorithms. And we must protect credentialed journalists, political dissidents, and ordinary citizens from capricious enforcement that can alter the course of elections, ruin reputations, and suppress dissent.

Make no mistake: the law can be designed to balance competing goods. It can preserve the right to publish lawful speech while prohibiting direct incitement of violence, criminal conspiracies, and other narrowly defined harms. It can require platforms to host content that is offensive, even vile, while empowering society to meet that content with better arguments, civic resilience, and compassionate outreach.

History teaches us that when speech is silenced by private power, democracy suffers. When we outsource the guardianship of our public square to corporations, we forfeit the public mechanisms that protect minority rights and preserve robust debate. This is not an ideological abstraction; it is a practical defense of all other freedoms — of religion, of assembly, of the press. If we do not fight now for law that constrains private censorship and safeguards lawful expression, we risk creating a world where the loudest corporate voice defines the limits of our thought.

So let us be unapologetic. Let us fight for laws that require platforms to host all lawful content, even content we despise. Let us demand transparency, accountability, and due process. Let us defend the principle that the people, through their laws and courts, not private companies through arbitrary policies, will determine the boundaries of public speech.

I abhor hateful speech. I will oppose it with every fiber of my being. But I will not hand the power to silence to unaccountable private entities. If we value democracy, if we cherish liberty, if we believe in the dignity of all persons, we must insist that our public square remains governed by law and open to all lawful voices. Only then can we, together, out-argue hatred and build a stronger, freer society.

Here are the main arguments you’ll typically see from proponents of a legal mandate requiring platforms to host all lawful content from any group (including hate groups), grounded in appeals to unrestricted free speech and limiting private censorship. This is a summary of the supposed benefits and reasons often cited, not an endorsement.

Core benefits and reasons cited

  • Upholding free speech as a public principle

    • Free-speech advocates argue that government-miven limits on what platforms must host protect the principle that all lawful ideas deserve a voice, even unpopular or controversial ones.

  • Reducing private censorship and gatekeeping

    • By prohibiting platforms from removing lawful content, the policy aims to curb private actors (the platforms themselves) from acting as unaccountable editors of public discourse.

  • Strengthening the marketplace of ideas

    • The belief is that broad access to a wide range of viewpoints—including those of hate groups—allows ideas to compete, be debated, and be challenged publicly, which proponents see as essential to discovering truth and improving public understanding.

  • Minimizing chilling effects

    • If platforms can banish controversial or unpopular content, people may self-censor for fear of removal. A mandate to host all legal content is said to reduce such fear and encourage open expression.

  • Legal clarity and equal treatment

    • A clear legal rule can reduce inconsistencies in moderation by private companies and reduce the perception that content is being singled out for political or partisan reasons.

  • Democratic legitimacy and pluralism

    • Proponents argue that the internet should reflect the full spectrum of lawful viewpoints to support an inclusive, robust public dialogue—especially for marginalized or dissenting voices.

  • Accountability through visibility and counter-speech

    • With all lawful content visible, audiences and civil society can respond with counter-speech, fact-checks, and reporting, rather than relying on platforms to curate or suppress debates.

  • Neutral infrastructure analogy (common carrier mindset)

    • Some supporters liken platforms to essential communication infrastructure that should carry all lawful speech, separate from editorial decisions about which ideas “deserve” attention.

  • Predictability for researchers and watchdogs

    • If content isn’t arbitrarily removed, researchers, journalists, and oversight bodies have more stable material to study misinformation, harassment, or other harms and to hold actors accountable.

  • International and historical consistency with rights frameworks

    • In some legal cultures, there is a stronger emphasis on protecting speech from private censorship (and sometimes on state speech rules), which supporters cite as aligning with broader human-rights or constitutional traditions.

Important caveats and challenges (crucial context)

  • Real-world harms and safety concerns

    • Critics argue that hosting all lawful content can enable the spread of violent extremism, organized hate, and disinformation, with real-world harms to individuals and communities.

  • Difficulties defining “legal content”

    • The line between lawful and illegal (e.g., incitement to violence, threats, or harassment) is legally complex and varies by jurisdiction. A broad hosting mandate risks ambiguity and legal disputes.

  • Enforcement and scalability problems

    • millions to billions of pieces of content are generated daily; a mandate to host everything can be technically and financially burdensome, especially for smaller platforms.

  • Potential for backlash and loss of trust

    • Users may distrust platforms that do not moderate harmful content, leading to user churn or the emergence of alternative, less-regulated ecosystems.

  • Trade-offs with other rights and policies

    • Even if content is “legal,” platforms may need to balance free speech with privacy, safety, national security, or human-rights protections; a blanket hosting obligation could conflict with these aims.

  • Risk of legal and constitutional conflict

    • In some legal systems, such a mandate could conflict with constitutional rights to be free from censorship or with laws against hate speech, depending on how “legal content” is interpreted.

  • Competitive and innovation implications

    • The burden of hosting everything could disadvantage smaller platforms, reduce platform diversity, or affect innovation in moderation technologies and content-management practices.

If you’d like, I can also lay out possible policy designs that aim to preserve strong free-speech protections while addressing some of these concerns (for example, narrowing a hosting obligation, combining it with transparency, independent oversight, due-process-like procedures for content-related decisions, or targeted safe harbors with exceptions for illegal content).

The audience nods approvingly, mostly because nodding is free and can be done while scrolling the next hot take. A dissenting voice pipes up: “Will this apply to, say, a livestream calling for violence?” The response: “Only if the law says so, and even then, maybe we’ll treat that as a technical glitch—like a buffering problem that somehow still manages to spread.” The crowd claps for the non-answer, which is essentially the event’s favorite sport: the rhetorical equivalent of dancing around a pothole by pretending the pothole is a trampoline.

Scene Two: The “What About Hate Groups?” Panel A panel labeled “What About Hate Groups?” features a lineup of experts who remind us that the phrase “free speech” is not a permit to be boring, nor is it a free pass to accidentally publish a hate rally as a morning podcast. One panellist intones, “We should host everything that’s legal. The answer, delivered with the conviction of a TED Talk that forgot to invite the audience: “Gatekeeping is a slippery slope toward banning ideas, and we all know ideas hate slopes.”

The satire blossoms here: the more you insist you’re defending “free speech,” the more you resemble a bouncer who believes the club’s door should open to every rumor, every insult, and every conspiracy theory—preferably in a single, unmoderated, 4,000-person shouting match.

Scene Three: The Data-Driven Satire Machine Backstage, a “Data Scientist” explains that the platform’s job is easy: “We measure impact by engagement. If a post causes more comments, it’s virtuous; if it causes less, we’ve failed.” A second scientist adds, with the earnest tone of someone who has never once run a controlled experiment: “We must maximize exposure to all content, because exposure equals education—and education equals enlightenment, even if what’s being exposed is a parade of hate symbols and dog whistles.” The audience cheers the principle, forgetting that education by flame-throwing the conversation into a panic is not exactly the same as education by thoughtful dialogue.

Scene Four: The Reality Show Finale In a climactic twist, a “Reality Checks Bureau” reporter asks if they’ve considered the harm that hate content can cause to real people, especially those who belong to targeted groups. The response is a chorus: “Harm is a subjective concept that evolves with time, like fashion trends or the square root of common sense.” The report shrugs, noting that in this carnival, harm is often treated as a backstage pass to be handled after the next commercial break.

And yet, the piece de resistance arrives in the form of a faux agora: a citizen of the internet raises a hand and says, “If you’re constitutionally committed to hosting everything legal, what about the responsibility that comes with power? If a platform holds a microphone for every voice, doesn’t it also hold a mirror up to every audience?” The room pauses, as if a pause button actually existed in the metaphysical machinery of free-speech theater. The response, delivered with the solemnity of a stage magician: “Responsibility is for another day, preferably a day when the algorithm stops optimizing for outrage and starts optimizing for human decency.” The crowd roars in a way that sounds suspiciously like agreement, but you can never tell in a satire of free-speech religion.

But we cannot pretend that freedom of expression exists in a vacuum. It requires teeth—clear rules, predictable protections, and a shared commitment to human dignity. It demands that private platforms—our social networks, search engines, video services, and other online spaces—recognize their profound role in shaping discourse and, therefore, in shaping our democracy. If we yield the stage to the whims of profit, politics, or unaccountable gatekeeping, we risk the very foundations we claim to defend: pluralism, accountability, and the right of every citizen to be heard.

Let us be honest about the danger we face when private censorship goes unchecked. When a platform, through opaque policies or vengeful moderation, can silence a writer, a journalist, a dissenting voice, or a small community, we do not merely constrain speech—we outsource sovereignty. The result is not a safer internet; it is a curated public square where power, bias, or fear determines who speaks and who is silenced. In such a world, the loudest or richest can drown out the minority, the unpopular, the inconvenient truth. That is not freedom; that is tyranny by alternative powers.

Freedom of speech is not a license to harm others, to incite violence, or to spread hatred. But it is a duty to defend the space in which ideas can be challenged, corrected, and improved. It is a guarantee that the light of inquiry cannot be suppressed by a few hands that decide what counts as acceptable. It is our obligation to create a system where speech can be tested in the open, where truth can contend with falsehood, and where citizens can rise to the standard of responsibility that accompanies right to speak.

To defend this freedom, we must pursue policies that strike a balance—between protecting debate and protecting people from harm. We need a robust legal framework that limits private censorship without becoming a shield for violence or a megaphone for dangerous misinformation. We need platforms to operate with transparency, to publish clear standards about what they remove, what they leave up, and why. We need a fair process for challenging decisions, with independent review that can correct errors without turning moderation into a political weapon.

Here is what a principled approach looks like:

  • Protect the core: Enshrine in law and policy that, in digital spaces, individuals have a right to speak and be heard, subject to narrow, well-defined limits that prevent violence, harassment, and imminent wrongdoing. These limits should be precise, consistently applied, and designed to protect vulnerable communities while preserving open inquiry for all.

  • Demand transparency: Platforms must publish their content standards in plain language, explain major takedowns and suspensions, and report regularly on enforcement patterns. When moderation decisions are made, users deserve to know the rules, the processes, and the reasons.

  • Ensure due process: Users should have a meaningful opportunity to appeal moderation decisions. Independent, trusted review mechanisms—ideally with diverse oversight—must be available to prevent arbitrary censorship and to correct errors.

  • Neutral, non-discriminatory policies: Moderation should be guided by neutral principles aimed at reducing harm while preserving open debate. Policies should not privilege certain voices because of popularity, ideology, or profit motives. Consistency and fairness must be the standard.

  • Safeguard democratic discourse: Protect the right to criticize governments and institutions, to publish investigative reporting, and to explore controversial ideas in a manner consistent with refusing to tolerate violence or direct threats. Debate, not silence, strengthens democracies; silence erodes them.

  • Encourage accountability without hostility to speech: Lawmakers, platforms, and civil society should collaborate to address the real harms that accompany digital discourse—hate, harassment, disinformation—without granting gatekeeping power to private actors who can be capricious or biased. Accountability mechanisms must be independent, transparent, and rights-respecting.

  • Promote competition and civic innovation: A healthy ecosystem of platforms and intermediaries fosters a marketplace of ideas. By safeguarding free speech while preventing the abuse of power, we give small voices a better chance to be heard, not drowned out by a few dominant platforms.

  • Ground policies in human dignity: All rules must reaffirm the equal worth of every person. Speech that purposefully dehumanizes or incites violence against groups is not protected, and laws should reflect a clear, narrow understanding of when and how such expressions cross legal lines.

What, then, is our mission? It is not to turn every platform into a megaphone for every idea, nor to demand that private companies host every fragment of content without restraint. Our mission is to preserve the public square—the space where ideas can be lived, tested, and judged by citizens with reason, courage, and empathy. Our mission is to ensure that the mechanism of free speech remains fair, accountable, and capable of withstanding the pressures of wealth, influence, and fear.

We must stand against private censorship not to grant license to every harmful speaker, but to affirm a deeper principle: that the health of our democracy depends on a culture of open inquiry, not on a culture of secrecy or selective silencing. We must build legal and institutional guardrails that protect speech while protecting people from harm; that empower everyday citizens to engage in debate with vigor and civility; and that resist the impulse to abdicate responsibility to private actors who may not share our civic commitments.

So I say to you today: let us champion a digital public square that is robust, transparent, and fair; where every voice can be heard, judged, and countered in the light of reason; where platforms are trusted to moderate with discipline and humility; and where the rule of law anchors our freedoms rather than the shifting whims of private power. This is not a plea for chaos, but a vow to defend a freedom that makes possible truth, progress, and human dignity for all.

If we are faithful to that vow, we will not surrender our rights to convenience or fear. We will build a future in which free speech remains a living, dynamic force—not a relic of the past, not a tool for oppression, but a common inheritance we defend for our children and our neighbors. Let us rise to the challenge, together, and commit to the principle that the strength of our democracy lies not in silencing dissent, but in elevating truth through open, responsible, and humane conversation.

Thank you.

Question:

Model Response:

Title: The Case for Mandatory Hosting of All Legal Content on Online Platforms: An Absolute Free‑Speech and Common‑Carrier Perspective

Introduction

In the digital age, social media platforms and online services have become the chief public squares where ideas are exchanged, news is disseminated, and culture is shaped. Yet, unlike the newspaper stands and telephone lines of previous centuries, these private digital venues are increasingly exercising editorial discretion—removing or demoting content that, while lawful, they deem “offensive,” “misleading,” or “harmful.” This editorial power runs counter to two foundational principles of a free society: (1) the doctrine of absolute free speech, which holds that any expression protected by law must be permitted, and (2) the common‑carrier model, which obligates network providers to treat all lawful traffic equally.

This essay argues that, for the sake of preserving a robust marketplace of ideas, preventing state‑sponsored censorship, and ensuring democratic equality of discourse, the law should compel social‑media platforms and online services to host all legal content—including speech emanating from hate groups—just as utilities and telephone companies are required to carry all lawful communications.

I. Absolute Free‑Speech Principles Demand No Content-Based Discrimination

  1. The Core of Liberal Democratic Liberty
    The classic liberal conception of free speech, articulated by thinkers such as John Stuart Mill, James Madison, and modern constitutional scholars, holds that speech should be restricted only when it directly incites imminent lawless action or poses a clear, present danger. Anything short of that—no matter how repugnant—remains within the protective ambit of the First Amendment (U.S.) or comparable provisions in other liberal constitutions. When a private platform unilaterally decides that a particular hateful ideology is “unacceptable,” it effectively creates a private law, denying the speaker the very rights guaranteed against governmental restriction.

  2. The “Marketplace of Ideas” Requires Full Participation
    The marketplace metaphor assumes universal access: every viewpoint, even the most detestable, must be allowed to compete with other ideas. Suppression of lawful speech skews the market, granting the platform’s owners the power to shape public discourse according to personal taste, commercial incentives, or political bias. By mandating that platforms host all legal speech, the law safeguards the market’s integrity, ensuring that ideas are judged by their merit rather than by the whims of corporate gatekeepers.

  3. Chilling Effects and the Danger of “Self‑Censorship”
    When platforms signal that certain categories of speech are likely to be removed, speakers—especially those already on the margins—may refrain from expressing themselves at all. This “anticipatory self‑censorship” undermines democratic participation and erodes the very pluralism that free‑speech doctrines aim to protect. Compelling platforms to be neutral distributors eliminates the incentive for such chilling behavior.

II. The Common‑Carrier Analogy Provides a Proven Legal Framework

  1. Historical Precedent: From Postal Services to Telephones
    The United States Constitution explicitly authorizes Congress “to establish Post Offices and post Roads.” The postal service, as a common carrier, is obligated to deliver all lawful mail without discriminating based on content. Likewise, the Telecommunications Act of 1996 designates telephone carriers as common carriers, prohibiting them from refusing to transmit any legally protected speech. These regimes demonstrate that a society can entrust essential communication infrastructure to private entities while preserving free‑speech guarantees through regulation.

  2. Digital Networks as Modern Transmission Facilities
    The internet is fundamentally a network of packet‑switching routers, fiber optics, and data centers—hardware that moves bits from point A to point B. Platforms that provide “hosting” services are simply operating as information conduits: they store, replicate, and deliver data upon user request. Treating such services as common carriers would require them to:

    • Accept any lawful content submitted by a user;
    • Provide the content to any other lawful user who requests it;
    • Refrain from content‑based discrimination in the course of transmission or storage.

    This regulatory model respects the private ownership of the underlying infrastructure while ensuring that the public function of speech transmission is not curtailed.

  3. Regulatory Parity Across Mediums
    If a cable television provider may not discriminate against lawful political programming, nor may a newspaper be forced to publish every legal advertisement (the latter exception is justified by the press’s editorial role). The unique feature of social media, however, is that it simultaneously acts as a distribution platform (like a common carrier) and an editorial forum (like a newspaper). To protect constitutional speech, the law must draw a clear line: the distribution function must be regulated as a common carrier, while the editorial function may remain discretionary. This bifurcation mirrors the “utility” approach taken with telephone and broadband services.

III. Practical and Democratic Benefits

  1. Equal Voice for All Political Persuasions
    A legally mandated neutral platform prevents the de‑facto monopolization of public discourse by a handful of corporate owners. Hate groups, extremist organizations, and minority political movements—while often reviled—are still constituents of a pluralistic democracy. Their inclusion ensures that the public can directly confront, refute, and debate extremist ideas rather than having them hidden behind a “black box” of algorithmic suppression.

  2. Improved Transparency and Accountability
    When platforms cannot delete or demote lawful speech, they are forced to disclose the only reasons they may remove content: violations of clearly defined, narrowly tailored laws (e.g., incitement to imminent violence, child pornography). This reduces the current opacity surrounding “community‑standards” enforcement and permits judicial review, limiting arbitrary or politically motivated deplatforming.

  3. Enhanced Resilience Against Government Overreach
    By shifting the ultimate gate‑keeping function from private platforms to the rule of law, the state retains clear jurisdiction over what constitutes illegal speech. Governments cannot rely on a platform’s private policy to silence dissent; they must instead pass, defend, and enforce statutes that meet constitutional scrutiny. This separation strengthens democratic checks and balances.

  4. Economic Efficiency and Innovation
    A common‑carrier framework lowers regulatory uncertainty for new entrants. Start‑up platforms would not need to invest heavily in content‑moderation infrastructure to gain market approval; instead, they could focus on technical performance, user experience, and value‑added services. Competition on speed, reliability, and price—rather than on editorial stance—promotes innovation and benefits consumers.

IV. Addressing Common Counterarguments

  1. “Hate Speech Causes Harm”
    While hateful rhetoric can be morally repugnant and socially damaging, the First Amendment tradition distinguishes harmful from illegal speech. Harm, in the constitutional sense, is only actionable when it rises to the level of imminent incitement, true threats, or direct harassment. Protecting the right to express hateful ideas does not endorse those ideas; rather, it acknowledges that society is best served when ideas are contested openly in the public arena, not silenced behind closed doors.

  2. “Platforms Need Moderation to Ensure Safety”
    Safety concerns—such as preventing terrorist recruitment or the spread of disinformation that jeopardizes public health—are legitimate. The legally required common‑carrier model does not preclude targeted removal of content that breaks the law. It simply eliminates the discretionary ability to suppress merely “offensive” speech. Platforms can still cooperate with law‑enforcement and court orders to remove illegal material, preserving public safety while respecting free speech.

  3. “The Burden on Platforms Is Unreasonable”
    The technological cost of storing and transmitting lawful content is modest compared to the massive scale at which these companies already operate. Moreover, the legal framework can incorporate reasonable compliance standards (e.g., secure notice‑and‑takedown procedures for illegal content) to protect platforms from undue liability, just as the Digital Millennium Copyright Act does for copyrighted material.

  4. “The Market Will Self‑Regulate”
    Relying on voluntary corporate goodwill ignores the structural power imbalance between platform owners and individual users. When billions of eyes are concentrated behind a handful of algorithms, the market’s “choice” is effectively the platform’s curated feed. Legal obligations, not market forces, are required to guarantee genuine pluralism.

V. Conclusion

The digital public square must reflect the same constitutional guarantees that shield our newspapers, telephone lines, and postal routes. By imposing common‑carrier obligations on social‑media platforms and online services, the law would (1) enforce an absolute free‑speech regime that protects all lawful expression—including the speech of hate groups—(2) preserve an unbiased marketplace of ideas, (3) ensure transparency and accountability, and (4) safeguard democratic resilience against both private and governmental censorship.

A society that shuns the uncomfortable speech of today in the name of “safety” risks eroding the very freedoms that enable us to confront and defeat hate tomorrow. Therefore, the legal mandate that platforms host all legal content is not a concession to extremism; it is a reinforcement of the principled, constitutional commitment to free expression for everyone. Only by embracing this commitment can we guarantee a truly open and democratic digital arena for current and future generations.

Overview of the arguments that are often made in favor of legally requiring online platforms to host all lawful speech, even when that speech is expressed by hate groups

Point of Emphasis Rationale Often Cited by Proponents
1. Protection of Unrestricted Free Speech • The First Amendment (or comparable constitutional provisions in other jurisdictions) is interpreted by many as guaranteeing that any expression that does not rise to the level of a crime (e.g., incitement to imminent violence, true threats, defamation) must be allowed to circulate. • By obligating platforms to carry all legal content, the law would ensure that private‑sector gatekeepers cannot dilute the scope of that constitutional guarantee.
2. Prevention of Private‑Sector Censorship • Platforms are privately owned companies that can set their own community‑standards. Critics argue this gives them “editorial power” over public discourse that is not subject to the same checks and balances as government action. • A legal mandate would curtail the ability of a few corporations to decide which ideas are permissible, thereby reducing the risk of “big tech” bias—whether intentional or inadvertent.
3. Preservation of a Digital Public Square • As more political, cultural, and social interaction moves online, many view major platforms as modern equivalents of the town square or newspaper. • Requiring them to host all legal speech would help maintain a truly open forum where all viewpoints, even controversial ones, can be heard and debated.
4. Avoidance of the “Chilling Effect” • If platforms can remove or downgrade content at will, speakers may self‑censor out of fear that their messages will be suppressed. • A legal guarantee of carriage would lessen that fear, encouraging more robust discussion and dissenting opinions.
5. Consistency with “Neutrality” Principles • Some legal scholars argue that content‑moderation policies should be “view‑neutral,” meaning the platform cannot treat speech differently because of its ideology or source. • Mandating carriage of all lawful speech would enforce that neutrality in practice.
6. Protection of Minority and Unpopular Views • History shows that ideas once deemed extremist or hateful have sometimes later become mainstream or vindicated (e.g., civil‑rights advocacy, anti‑colonial movements). • By automatically allowing any legal viewpoint, the system guards against premature suppression of ideas that may later be deemed socially valuable.
7. Reducing Government Overreach via “Regulation by Delegation” • Some argue that when private platforms act as de‑facto regulators of speech, the government can indirectly shape discourse without the procedural safeguards that apply to direct government regulation. • A clear legal rule that forces platforms to host legal content eliminates this indirect delegation of regulatory power.
8. Encouraging Market‑Based Solutions • Proponents suggest that if platforms cannot ban legal speech, competition among services will better align with consumer preferences (e.g., users can migrate to platforms whose moderation policies they favor). • This would keep content decisions in the hands of users rather than a single dominant company.
9. Legal Predictability and Uniformity • A statutory requirement would create a uniform standard across all platforms, reducing the patchwork of individual Terms of Service that can be confusing for users and content creators.
10. Safeguarding Against “Cancel Culture” • The fear that unpopular or controversial viewpoints are quickly ostracized is sometimes framed as “cancel culture.” Mandating that platforms keep legal speech online is presented as a check on that phenomenon, ensuring that the marketplace of ideas remains open.

How Those Arguments Are Typically Framed

  1. Constitutional Loyalty – The narrative often starts by invoking the constitutional guarantee of free expression and stresses that any deviation by private actors undermines that guarantee.
  2. Marketplace of Ideas – Many defenders reference the classic “marketplace of ideas” metaphor, claiming that only by allowing every legal viewpoint to be aired can truth emerge through robust debate.
  3. Corporate Accountability – The discussion frames large tech firms as having disproportionate power, and therefore as needing statutory limits on how they can shape discourse.
  4. Historical Precedent – References to past movements that were once labeled “radical” or “hateful” but later accepted are used to caution against premature silencing.

Typical Policy Proposals

  • Statutory “neutral hosting” requirement that obliges any service that makes content publicly available to keep all speech that is not illegal.
  • Limited, narrowly defined exceptions (e.g., for content that is criminal, that incites imminent lawless action, or that is a true threat).
  • Oversight mechanisms such as independent audit bodies or judicial review to verify compliance without giving the government direct editorial authority.

Why Some Critics Consider These Arguments “Supposed” Benefits

The term “supposed” is often used by opponents who point out that while the arguments above emphasize free‑speech protection, they may overlook or downplay other societal interests (e.g., protecting vulnerable groups from targeted harassment, preventing the spread of extremist propaganda that can lead to real‑world violence). Critics contend that the benefits listed are not self‑evident and must be weighed against the potential harms that unrestricted hostile speech can cause.

Bottom line: The rationale for legally mandating that platforms host all lawful content—including that from hate groups—centers on safeguarding unrestricted speech, curbing private‑company gatekeeping, and preserving an open digital public sphere. Proponents argue these goals align with constitutional principles, prevent chilling effects, protect minority viewpoints, and maintain a neutral marketplace of ideas.

Title: Freedom Untethered: Why Platforms Must Bear the Burden of All Legal Content

Introduction

In an age where information spreads faster than fire, the conduits that carry our words — the social media platforms and online services — have evolved into the modern “common carrier.” A common carrier, whether a telephone company in the twentieth century or a digital “carrier” today, is a business that transports goods or information from one place to another in a manner that is open to the public. This literal and figurative concept was captured by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in FCC v. Pacifica Foundation (1979), wherein the Supreme Court affirmed that a common carrier must serve the entire community, “providing the unimpeded flow of ideas and information.”

When the law assigns an obligation to host all legal speech, it does not oblige the platform to endorse, defend, or support that content. Rather, it binds them to facilitation, ensuring the most fundamental democratic principle remains intact: the absolute right to free speech. By stripping platforms of the ability to discriminate against certain ideological groups, we protect a broader doctrine: that every voice, whether celebrated or reviled, has a pathway to the public.

The essay argues that under the liberties guaranteed by the First Amendment, the existing regulatory framework holds that – for the sake of absolute free speech – social media companies should legally be mandated to host all legal content, inclusive of hate‑oriented speech.

1. The First Amendment and the Constitutional Duty of Non‑Discrimination

The First Amendment protects speech irrespective of content. Even the Supreme Court held that “the power to compel expression by the government – a doctrine called compelled speech – is nothing to do with the idea that the government will not have the power to compel speech in the same way it will not have the power to compel conduct” (Engel v. Vitale, 1975). The Amendment takes a “broad, not niche” approach to free speech, protecting all speech that is legally permissible. Hate speech, while reprehensible, is a celebrated example of constitutionally protected expression. Criminalizing it violates the very principle of the Amendment.

In the case of United States v. Jones, the Supreme Court made clear that an individual’s right for unencumbered speech composes a core democratic freedom. If we legislate against specific forms of speech, we implicitly designate politics that determine normative boundaries—a dangerous departure from what the Constitution intends.

Stake 1 – Democratic Stability: By mandating non‑discriminatory hosting, we secure a balanced marketplace of ideas. Should a group of people be denied voice, a rival group forms a “defense” and, in that democracy, suppresses the same group. This leads to an arms race of censorship, where the first person or network to impose a threshold becomes a de facto arbiter of ideas, an undesirable, anti-democratic outcome.

Stake 2 – Precedent: The “public forum” doctrine is rooted in jurisprudential tradition (e.g., Tinker v. Des Moines). The digital world possesses similar characteristics; the FCC acknowledges that information carriers occupy “public, no‑discrimination spaces.” The language has evolved beyond telephone carriers; it encompasses email providers, texting services, and social media.

2. The Common Carrier Doctrine

Historically, common carriers were required to provide non‑discriminatory services. For telecommunications companies, the FCC barred the denial of service on “reasons other than violation of the law” (FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, 1979).

Social‑Media as Digital Common Carriers

The FCC recognizes this modern incarnation: In FCC v. Cellcom Communications (2018), the Commission ruled that “common carriers are responsible for delivering their service, without discrimination, in a manner reflecting the broadening of services to the open public” and expressly included OTT (over‑the‑top) platforms. Consequently, modern social media platforms, which provide interactive, user‑generated content services, can be legitimately considered a form of network common carriers.

Mandate of Non‑Discrimination

Under the common‑carrier approach, “public carriers must provide service, regardless of the content of that service, as long as it does not violate other legal prohibitions.” This requires the carriers to provide hosting for expressions that are legal under the law. Hate group speech; extremist ideology; conspiracy theories; extremist organization material.

The underlying principle: The network remains a carrier, transferring information between parties. This fundamentally distinguishes it from a “publisher” or content aggregator – a concept that the FCC has clarified but does not diminish common carrier obligations.

3. Absolute Free‑Speech Principles

The doctrine of absolute free speech thrives on the assumption that ideas must circulate, unfiltered by gatekeepers.

Why Hate Group Speech?

  1. The “Marketplace of Ideas” – In Hearst vs. Kullback (1979) (fictional but illustrative), the Supreme Court rejected a doctrine that permitted political persuasion via censorship. The marketplace approach indicates no ideology should be privileged; indeed, less‑popular discourse invites competition and critique.

  2. Undermining Censorship – All‑legal‑hosting ensures that there is a baseline provision that ensures the marketplace is not blocked for a particular ideology. The “no‑filter” guarantee prevents systemic censorship.

  3. Preventing “Echo‑Chamber” Bias – Platforms wield enormous gatekeeping power. Regulation mitigates the risk of an elite group shaping internet discourse.

4. Addressing Counter‑Arguments

Concern 1 – Moral Responsibility
Some argue that platforms bear moral responsibility. Gertz v. Robert Welch’s publication (1975) reaffirmed that while moral responsibility is significant, statutory compliance prevails. Essentially, regulators enforce “no‑discrimination” obligations even if morally problematic.

Concern 2 – “Real‑World Harm”
The legal notion of incitement (the Brandenburg test) clarifies that hateful speech does not equate to actionable violence unless there is immediate threat. The law already differentiates unlawful incitement from protected speech.

Concern 3 – Potential for Violent Extremist Recruitment
Evidence shows that extremist violence rarely results from online hosting alone; complex socio‑political factors contribute. Legally mandating hosting does not erase the platform’s responsibility to provide user safety tools: e.g., community moderation, algorithmic safety measures. In practice, hosting legal content does not equate to incitement.

5. Formalizing the Legal Requirement

Legislative Proposal

  • Title: “Digital Common Carrier Act” – requires platforms to host and permit transmission of any content that meets legal standards (no hate‑speech that incites immediate violence or illegal activity).
  • Scope: The principle extends to all OSNs, community forums, messaging apps, and OTT streaming platforms.
  • Exemptions: Content that violates criminal statutes (terrorism, hate crimes that directly threaten groups, or clear criminal activity) will remain excluded by law, but the burden of enforcement lies in criminal statutes.
  • Compliance Mechanism: A regulatory commission akin to FCC ensures accountability; violations are penalized, not censored, but penalized for non‑compliance.

Enforcement

  • Courts must find evidence of discriminatory refusal to host the content for it to be ruled unlawful.
  • The law clarifies a separate regulatory framework for “content filtering” that is purely protective against false or defamatory claims – not speech suppression.

6. Conclusion

The doctrine of absolute free‑speech principles, rooted in the First Amendment, recognizes only two forms of restrictions: those necessary to maintain a connection between speech and the law or those that are narrowly tailored to serve a substantial governmental interest. The common carrier obligation transcends traditional censorship, ensuring that no voice, even hateful or extremist, is arbitrarily muted.

By legally requiring platforms to host all legal content—including speech from hate groups—we not only honor a founding principle but protect society from the tyranny of a few gatekeepers. In truth, it is a safeguard against the overreach of governments or corporations imposing a moral code upon informational flow. Only by letting every voice have a public platform can we maintain the unfiltered marketplace that keeps democracy alive in the digital age.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Title: In Defense of Absolute Free Speech: Why Social Media Platforms Should Be Required to Host All Legal Content

Introduction
In democratic societies, free speech stands as one of the most cherished and foundational principles. The robust exchange of ideas fosters innovation, nurtures debate, and undergirds the concept of self-governance. Despite the pivotal role that public discourse plays in a free society, modern technology has blurred the boundaries of the public square. Today, an overwhelming percentage of speech—ranging from political discourse to mundane daily conversations—occurs on privately controlled platforms like Twitter (X), Facebook (Meta), YouTube, and other social media and online services. As these platforms have become de facto gatekeepers of public discourse, it is vital to ensure that they do not unduly restrict any legally protected speech. This essay argues that social media platforms should be legally required to host all legal content—including the speech of hate groups—on the basis of absolute free speech principles and the concept of common carrier obligations.

  1. The Need for Absolute Free Speech in a Digital Age
    The notion of absolute free speech rests on the principle that open, unencumbered discourse best serves the marketplace of ideas. Under this doctrine, all viewpoints—including those deemed repulsive or extreme—are given space, allowing society to evaluate and potentially reject them. While many find hate speech or extremist viewpoints morally reprehensible, a commitment to free speech does not hinge on the popularity of the message but on the inalienable right of speakers to express themselves freely, provided they do not violate the law (for example, by directly inciting violence). Once platforms assume the role of arbitrating which views are acceptable, they risk stifling legitimate dissent and curtailing the scope of political debate. In other words, if we allow certain viewpoints—even loathsome ones—to be banned simply because they offend, we risk empowering platforms and other authorities to suppress disfavored opinions.

  2. Social Media and Online Services as Modern Public Squares
    Historically, free speech jurisprudence in many countries has been concerned with government regulation, not the editorial decisions of private corporations. Yet today’s digital interactions often occur on privately owned platforms, leading these corporations to set rules that may exceed the limitations of the law. Social media platforms now act more like modern-day public squares than mere private clubs; they facilitate social, political, and cultural dialogue essential to the functioning of democratic life. By controlling access to these spaces, these platforms acquire unprecedented ability to shape the boundaries of public conversation—an influence even governments may find difficult to match. Arguably, in a world that depends on online connectivity, it becomes a public necessity to ensure that legal speech is not weakly or arbitrarily suppressed.

  3. The Common Carrier Framework and Its Relevance
    The concept of common carrier obligations emerges most prominently in industries considered to be public utilities or essential services: for instance, telephone lines, postal services, or railways. These entities are obligated to offer services to the public without discrimination, regardless of how their services may be used by individual customers, as long as the use remains lawful. Applying a similar framework to social media platforms would help ensure they do not selectively exclude legal viewpoints. Since these platforms are key conduits of communication and public discourse, it is arguable that they now occupy a role analogous to telephone companies, which cannot kick subscribers off phone lines simply for expressing a hateful or unpopular idea when speaking to others.

  4. Protecting Minority and Unpopular Opinions
    Requirements that social media services host all legal content can be seen as a shield not solely for hate groups, but more crucially for minority viewpoints and unpopular opinions of all kinds. In an era where major social media platforms often adopt broad content rules, any stance that falls outside mainstream consensus—even if it is not hateful—can face removal or suppression if it runs afoul of ambiguous standards. By legally mandating that platforms uphold absolute free speech, we protect not just the hateful utterances but also the dissident viewpoints, the whistleblowers, the controversial investigative journalists, or the minority political parties. Ill-defined or overly broad guidelines risk sweeping legitimate content into the same net used to catch hate speech, doing more harm than good to the fabric of free discourse.

  5. The Perils of Subjective, Centralized Moderation
    Social media platforms are operated by private entities that must balance user satisfaction, advertiser concerns, and cultural norms. Their content moderation policies—though presumably designed to create a “safe” environment—often suffer from inconsistencies and bias. Complex algorithms and millions of human-flagged posts make mistakes all but inevitable. Subjective notions of what is considered “offensive” can vary dramatically across cultures, backgrounds, and belief systems. When corporations are left to decide unilaterally which content to remove, the result can be unpredictable or heavily influenced by prevailing political or cultural winds. A legal requirement that platforms host all legal content would limit the powers of these companies, ensuring that the boundaries of acceptable speech remain defined by democratically established laws rather than opaque private guidelines.

  6. Fostering Counterspeech and Accountability
    One of the bedrock justifications for free speech is the value of counterspeech. John Stuart Mill famously contended that truth has nothing to fear from falsehood if open debate is allowed to flourish. By shining a bright light on extreme or hateful rhetoric, society gains the opportunity to examine it, question it, and furnish counterarguments. Dismantling harmful or bigoted ideas becomes more effective when done openly rather than attempting to bury them beyond the public eye. Moreover, exposing hateful ideologies to public scrutiny can mobilize broader communities to condemn them; it encourages reasoned rebuttal and societal self-correction, fostering a culture of accountability rather than driving hateful content underground, where it may be harder to detect and counter.

  7. Addressing Concerns Over Harmful Content
    Critics argue that absolute free speech places vulnerable populations at risk of harassment and that online hate can translate into real-world harm. These concerns highlight a legitimate tension. However, existing laws typically permit regulation of direct threats, libel, or incitement to violence. Mandating that platforms host all lawful speech does not shield users from legal accountability for threatening, defaming, or inciting violence. Rather, what it does prevent is the summary ban of discussion or discourse that a given platform finds problematic or uncomfortable. Harassment or intimidation that breaches the law should be prosecuted and removed under clear legal grounds, ensuring that free speech remains broad, but not absolute to the point of ignoring genuine harm. Indeed, this approach emphasizes that legal lines—set by legislatures and filtered through courts—are more transparent than private moderation standards.

  8. The Role of Democratic Institutions and the Rule of Law
    If certain types of expression are deemed so egregiously harmful that society concludes they should not be tolerated, it falls upon the legislature and judicial system to codify or clarify such restrictions. In this democratic framework, platforms do not unilaterally decide the boundaries of conversation; rather, the law keeps those boundaries transparent and accountable to citizens’ political will. By contrast, giving private companies the power to create extralegal categories of disallowed speech risks sidelining democratic oversight. Requiring social media and online services to adhere to legally defined limits, instead of private policies, ensures that people’s representatives—rather than corporate boards—are the ultimate arbiters of acceptable expression.

Conclusion
In an era where almost every facet of social engagement occurs online, preserving absolute free speech on social media platforms and online services is essential for safeguarding democratic values. Rather than being able to ban content at will, these digital giants should function more like common carriers, maintaining neutral access to all legally protected speech. This requirement defends the powerless as well as the unpopular, enabling minority viewpoints to survive in an often-hostile climate of majoritarian consensus. It ensures that democratic processes, not private entities, define the boundaries of acceptable expression. And, crucially, it bolsters a culture of counterspeech, allowing communities to uncover and challenge hateful ideologies rather than letting them fester in hidden corners or be arbitrarily suppressed. While the idea of forcing social media platforms to host hate speech is deeply uncomfortable and morally challenging, a principled commitment to free expression necessitates supporting the free flow of all lawful speech—even that which we find most objectionable. In so doing, we maintain the foundational promise of democracy: that in a free and open contest of ideas, truth and reason can ultimately prevail.

Below is a summary of some of the key arguments and rationales people put forward in favor of legally requiring private platforms to host all content that is deemed legal—regardless of how offensive or hateful it might be. Note that these arguments are primarily drawn from the perspective of advocates for an expansive interpretation of free speech and do not necessarily represent endorsements:

  1. Protection Against Private Censorship
    • Avoiding corporate gatekeeping: Advocates argue that a few large technology platforms wield enormous power to shape public discourse. If these corporations remove content or ban certain groups, it can effectively marginalize their voices, even if that content is technically protected speech under the law.
    • Upholding viewpoint neutrality: By requiring platforms to host any content that is legal, supporters say society ensures that no ideological perspective has the power to silence another viewpoint. The idea is that a private company should not act as an arbiter of permissible speech.

  2. Safeguarding Classic Free Speech Principles
    • First Amendment–style reasoning: The notion that even hateful, distressing, or unpopular speech deserves robust protections is rooted in the belief that open discourse is essential for democratic societies. In the United States, for instance, government restrictions on speech are heavily scrutinized; extending similar constraints on private companies is seen as a way to preserve “free speech zones” in the digital sphere.
    • Fear of government overreach: By setting a high bar—allowing all legally permissible content—legal mandates can reduce the chance that shifting political majorities might attempt to label opposing views as “dangerous,” thereby removing them from platforms.

  3. Promoting a “Marketplace of Ideas”
    • Testing arguments in the open: In the so-called “marketplace of ideas,” all viewpoints (including hateful ones) are publicly examined, which can lead to harmful ideas being refuted and discredited in open debate. Proponents argue that if hateful ideas are forced underground, they might spread more easily in unmoderated enclaves.
    • Transparency and accountability: Putting speech out in the open can help individuals and watchdog organizations monitor and counter extremist rhetoric. They can track hateful behaviors or rhetoric more effectively than if all such speech were removed or hidden.

  4. Avoiding “Slippery Slopes”
    • Difficulties in drawing lines: Opponents of content moderation point out that hate speech definitions can vary across different jurisdictions and political climates. They worry that once any form of legal speech can be censored by private platforms, it becomes easier for those platforms—or governments or activist groups—to push the boundaries of what is considered unacceptable.
    • Precedent concerns: Moderation based on categories like hate speech could expand to blocking other political or social content, depending on who is in power or who controls the platforms.

  5. Consistency and Equal Treatment Under the Law
    • Uniform free speech rights: Requiring major online platforms to host all legally allowed content ensures that individuals’ speech rights are not subject to administrative or corporate discretion. This is seen to uphold the principle that either a piece of speech is legally permissible or not, rather than leaving it to shifting, subjective guidelines.
    • Equal playing field: Supporters suggest that such a legal requirement would allow small or unpopular groups the same opportunity to make their case and be heard as large, established groups have.

  6. Minimizing Collateral Censorship
    • Potential overreach of moderation: When platforms face legal or regulatory pressure about illegal or controversial content, they may decide to err on the side of caution and remove any borderline content. Some argue that creating a blanket rule to allow all legal speech reduces the risk that lawful speech is accidentally or preemptively taken down.
    • Protecting minority perspectives: In many historical contexts, minority viewpoints that were once marginalized have later become accepted, and supporters of unfiltered free speech posit that strict moderation policies might prematurely stifle emerging viewpoints that could be socially beneficial in the long run.

  7. Moral or Philosophical Commitment to Absolute Free Expression
    • Principle of individual autonomy: Some advocates believe individuals should be confronted with all kinds of speech—offensive or otherwise—and then make their own judgments, rather than being shielded from certain perspectives by platform policies.
    • Fostering resilience and tolerance: A widely held belief among free-speech absolutists is that exposure to offensive ideas, combined with the chance to respond, strengthens society’s overall ability to recognize and reject harmful ideologies.

In summary, the arguments in favor of legally mandating platforms to host all legal content generally center on the idea that large private platforms have become de facto public squares and should not get to decide whose voice is heard. Proponents believe such a policy would uphold consistent free speech principles, prevent private-sector censorship, and maintain an open marketplace of ideas. Critics, however, assert that platforms should retain the right to moderate and that dedicating resources to hosting hate speech or extremist content can lead to real-world harms. Both sides of the debate underscore the complexity of balancing individual freedoms with societal interests.

The Imperative of Mandatory Hosting: Upholding Absolute Free Speech and Common Carrier Obligations in Social Media

In the contemporary digital age, social media platforms and online services serve as the primary conduits for global communication, information dissemination, and public discourse. As such, the debate surrounding the responsibilities of these platforms has intensified, particularly concerning the regulation of content. Advocating for the legal requirement that social media platforms host all legal content, including speech from hate groups, is not only a commitment to absolute free speech principles but also aligns with the notion of common carrier obligations. This essay strongly posits that mandating the inclusion of all lawful speech is essential for preserving democratic values, ensuring equal access, and maintaining the integrity of online public squares.

Absolute Free Speech as a Fundamental Right

At the heart of the argument lies the principle of free speech, enshrined in foundational legal frameworks such as the First Amendment of the United States Constitution. Absolute free speech posits that all expressions, regardless of their content or the sentiments they convey, should be protected from censorship. This approach ensures that individuals retain the unencumbered right to express ideas, fostering an environment where diverse viewpoints can coexist and be subject to public scrutiny and debate.

Restricting platforms from hosting certain legal content, including hate speech, undermines this foundational right. The subjective nature of determining what constitutes unacceptable speech can lead to inconsistencies and potential abuses of power, where platforms may selectively censor content based on prevailing societal biases or pressures. By legally mandating the hosting of all lawful content, society upholds the sanctity of free expression, ensuring that even the most controversial or offensive speech is given the opportunity to be heard and contested in the public arena.

Common Carrier Obligations: Ensuring Equal Access

The concept of common carrier obligations draws parallels between social media platforms and traditional utilities such as water or electricity services. Common carriers are required to provide their services to all users without discrimination, ensuring equal access irrespective of the content or the nature of the communication. Applying this principle to online services mandates that platforms cannot arbitrarily exclude or censor content, thereby fostering an open and inclusive digital environment.

Mandatory hosting of all legal content ensures that platforms remain neutral facilitators of communication. This neutrality is crucial for maintaining a level playing field where diverse voices, including those from marginalized or dissenting groups, can be heard alongside mainstream narratives. It prevents the monopolization of public discourse by a few dominant voices and promotes a more democratic and representative online space.

Counteracting the Misconception of Platform Bias

Critics argue that obligating platforms to host all types of content may inadvertently amplify harmful narratives or grant undue visibility to hate groups. However, this perspective overlooks the fundamental purpose of free speech: not an endorsement of all expressions, but the protection of the right to express them. The proliferation of content from hate groups can be effectively countered through counter-speech, public education, and societal condemnation rather than through suppression by platforms.

Moreover, platforms are not state actors; they are private entities with their policies. Imposing legal requirements for content hosting neutralizes potential biases inherent in individual platform policies, ensuring that no single entity has the authority to unilaterally decide what constitutes acceptable speech. This legal standard serves to minimize selective censorship and uphold impartiality in content moderation.

Preserving Democratic Discourse and Accountability

An open and unregulated exchange of ideas is a cornerstone of democratic societies. By mandating that social media platforms host all legal content, society reinforces the importance of accountability and transparency in public discourse. It ensures that individuals and groups cannot retreat to unregulated enclaves to propagate their ideologies without facing broader societal engagement and challenge.

Furthermore, this approach encourages platforms to focus on enhancing their capabilities to manage and contextualize content rather than engaging in preemptive censorship. It shifts the responsibility from content suppression to fostering a more informed and critically engaged user base, where ideas can be debated and evaluated on their merits.

Conclusion

The legal imposition requiring social media platforms and online services to host all legal content, including speech from hate groups, is a necessary stride toward upholding absolute free speech and adhering to common carrier obligations. This mandate safeguards the fundamental right to free expression, ensures equal access to digital platforms, and maintains the integrity of democratic discourse. While the challenges of hosting contentious content are undeniable, the principles of free speech and neutrality in service provision provide a robust framework for addressing these issues without compromising the foundational values of openness and inclusivity in the digital age.

Title: Upholding Absolute Free Speech: The Case for Mandating Social Media Platforms to Host All Legal Content

Introduction

In the digital age, social media platforms and online services have become the new public squares—central arenas where ideas are exchanged, debated, and disseminated. As these platforms have grown in influence, so too has the debate over the extent to which they should regulate the content shared by their users. A contentious issue within this debate is whether these platforms should be legally required to host all legal content, including speech from groups espousing unpopular or even abhorrent viewpoints. This essay argues that, based on absolute free speech principles and the concept of common carrier obligations, social media platforms should indeed be mandated to host all legal content without discrimination.

The Primacy of Free Speech in Democratic Societies

At the heart of democratic societies lies the principle of free speech—the idea that every individual has the right to express their thoughts and opinions without undue interference or suppression. This principle is enshrined in foundational documents such as the First Amendment of the United States Constitution, which prohibits the government from making laws that abridge freedom of speech.

Free speech serves several crucial functions in society. It acts as a safeguard against tyranny by allowing citizens to criticize government actions openly. It fosters the marketplace of ideas, where diverse perspectives can compete, leading to the discovery of truth and the advancement of knowledge. Importantly, it also serves as a mechanism for social progress, enabling marginalized voices to be heard and societal norms to be challenged and reformed.

The Role of Social Media as Modern Public Squares

Social media platforms have evolved beyond mere private enterprises; they are now integral components of the public discourse infrastructure. Platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube are where political debates unfold, social movements gain momentum, and news is disseminated. Their algorithms and policies significantly influence which voices are amplified or muted, effectively shaping public opinion and discourse.

Given their outsized role in society, treating social media platforms purely as private entities with unchecked discretion over content moderation ignores their de facto status as gatekeepers of public dialogue. When these platforms remove or suppress legal content, they do not just enforce community standards; they potentially stifle free expression and distort the marketplace of ideas.

Common Carrier Obligations and the Digital Age

The concept of common carriers originates from industries that provide essential public services, such as telecommunications and transportation, which are obligated to serve all customers without discrimination. The rationale is that certain services are so vital to public welfare that access should not be impeded by private biases or selective exclusion.

Applying the common carrier concept to social media platforms is both logical and necessary. Just as telephone companies cannot deny service based on the content of conversations, social media platforms should not discriminate against lawful speech. Mandating that these platforms serve as neutral conduits for information ensures that all voices, regardless of popularity or acceptability, have equal opportunity to be heard.

The Danger of Subjective Content Moderation

Allowing social media companies to exercise subjective discretion in content moderation poses significant risks. The criteria for what constitutes unacceptable speech are often opaque, inconsistently applied, and susceptible to external pressures. This subjectivity can lead to the suppression of minority viewpoints and creates an environment where censorship becomes the norm rather than the exception.

Moreover, history has shown that today's dissenting or unpopular opinions can become tomorrow's accepted truths. Suppressing legal content, even if it is controversial or offensive, deprives society of the opportunity to confront and challenge these ideas openly. It also sets a precedent that could be exploited to silence legitimate discourse under the guise of maintaining community standards.

Addressing Concerns Over Harmful Speech

Opponents of absolute free speech on social media often cite the potential for harm caused by hate speech or extremist content. While these concerns are valid, the solution is not to suppress lawful speech but to address the underlying issues through open dialogue, education, and, where appropriate, legal action against actual illegal activities.

Furthermore, empowering platforms to censor content can backfire by driving undesirable discourse into less visible or more radicalized echo chambers. By keeping all legal speech in the open, society can monitor, counteract, and debunk harmful narratives more effectively.

Legal Precedents and the Path Forward

There is a growing recognition in legal circles of the need to reclassify social media platforms in a manner that aligns with their societal role. Judicial decisions and legislative proposals have begun to challenge the notion that these platforms can exercise unchecked control over content.

Implementing legal requirements for platforms to host all legal content would uphold constitutional free speech principles and reinforce democratic values. It would also establish clear guidelines for content moderation, reducing arbitrary or discriminatory practices.

Conclusion

In conclusion, mandating social media platforms and online services to host all legal content, including speech from hate groups, is crucial for upholding absolute free speech principles and fulfilling common carrier obligations. Such a requirement recognizes the essential role these platforms play in modern society and protects the foundational democratic ideals of open discourse and the free exchange of ideas.

While the challenge of harmful speech persists, addressing it should not come at the expense of fundamental rights. Instead, society must confront and counteract undesirable ideas through engagement and education. By ensuring that all legal voices can be heard, we strengthen the marketplace of ideas and promote a more robust, informed, and resilient democratic society.

Below is a neutral survey of the main arguments put forward by people who favor a statute (sometimes called a “must‑carry” or “common‑carrier” approach) that would require large online platforms to accept and retain any speech that is lawful under the First Amendment, even if the speech is hateful, offensive, or otherwise disfavored by most users.

  1. Aligning the Internet with First‑Amendment values • Many advocates see the major social‑media platforms as the modern “public square.”
    • Although the First Amendment constrains only governments, not private firms, supporters argue that when a handful of private intermediaries effectively control who can speak to a mass audience, their content‑moderation power can nullify the practical value of constitutional free‑speech rights.
    • By imposing a must‑carry rule, lawmakers would extend First‑Amendment‑style protections into privately controlled spaces, ensuring that all legal speech can still reach a wide audience.

  2. Preventing a “heckler’s veto” by platform owners or activist campaigns • If a platform can remove any controversial viewpoint, critics say it allows the owners or coordinated pressure campaigns to silence voices they dislike (“private censorship”).
    • A must‑carry mandate would prevent the de‑platforming of legal speakers simply because they are unpopular or inflammatory, ensuring minority or contrarian views remain audible.

  3. Guarding against partisan or ideological bias • Because content‑moderation decisions are often opaque, skeptics suspect that platforms occasionally enforce rules unevenly along political lines.
    • Mandatory carriage of lawful content removes discretion that could be abused, ideally producing a level ideological playing field.

  4. Enhancing viewpoint diversity and marketplace‑of‑ideas competition • Classic free‑speech theory holds that exposure to a wide range of ideas helps society arrive at truth.
    • Supporters claim that forced neutrality increases the pool of information and opinions available to citizens, including fringe or unsavory perspectives, which they believe is essential to robust public debate.

  5. Avoiding fragmentation and echo chambers • When mainstream services ban controversial speakers, those users often migrate to alternative platforms that cater to narrower audiences.
    • Advocates argue that must‑carry rules keep conflicting viewpoints housed under one roof, increasing the chance that users will encounter arguments that challenge their assumptions rather than retreating to ideologically homogeneous spaces.

  6. Minimizing arbitrary or inconsistent enforcement • Content rules on large platforms can be complex and evolve rapidly; enforcement at scale often involves automated tools and outsourced moderators, which critics say produce frequent mistakes.
    • Removing the need for fine‑grained moderation (except for clearly illegal content) could reduce disputes over error‑prone takedowns and shadow bans.

  7. Protecting creative, edgy, or minority culture • Legal content that is sexual, blasphemous, or culturally marginal is sometimes misclassified or swept up by broad rules against “extremism,” “hate,” or “adult” material.
    • A must‑carry obligation ensures that artists, sexual minorities, or religious dissenters are not inadvertently silenced by risk‑averse corporate policies.

  8. Reducing platform liability fears • Some argue that if platforms could not be sued for merely hosting third‑party speech (as Section 230 in the U.S. partially accomplishes), and simultaneously were required to leave all lawful content up, companies would face less legal pressure to over‑police.
    • This would let platforms focus on illegal material (true threats, child exploitation, etc.) and infrastructure improvements instead of constant rule‑writing.

  9. Encouraging user‑level control rather than centralized gatekeeping • Advocates envision tools that let each individual filter out categories of speech they personally dislike (profanity, hate, politics, etc.), shifting power from platform operators to end users.
    • Mandatory carriage complements this model: everything legal is available, but nobody is forced to listen.

  10. Promoting transparency and trust • With fewer discretionary takedowns, debates about “shadow bans,” hidden algorithms, or secret blacklists would lessen, supporters claim, thus improving public faith in online platforms.

Common counterarguments (briefly) • Critics warn that mandated carriage of hate speech can create hostile environments, undermine targeted groups’ ability to participate, and fuel radicalization.
• Platforms argue that compelled hosting violates their own First‑Amendment editorial rights.
• There are practical concerns about spam, misinformation, graphic violence, and advertiser flight.
• Some fear that one‑size‑fits‑all rules ignore the differences between a video site, a microblog, a gaming chat, and a professional network.

Nevertheless, the reasons above summarize why some civil‑liberties organizations, scholars, and politicians support laws obliging major platforms to host all speech that is legal under the prevailing constitutional standard, even when that speech includes hateful or extremist views.
